h1: North American P-51 Mustang: Designed in 117 Days, Transformed by a Merlin
description: The P-51 Mustang went from a British order to a finished airframe in 117 days, and more than 14,000 were built. Its Merlin engine, specs and sources.
intro: The North American P-51 Mustang was the long-range escort fighter of the Second World War's final two years, and it started as a rush job for someone else. In 1940, British purchasing agents asked North American Aviation to build Curtiss P-40s under license. The company offered an original design instead and promised it in under three months.

The first airframe, the NA-73, was finished 117 days later. Its first flight came in October 1940: Boeing's history, which now holds North American's records, gives October 26, while the Smithsonian gives October 25. The Royal Air Force ordered 150 and named it Mustang.
More than 14,000 were built. The definitive P-51D, with a cut-down rear fuselage, a bubble canopy and six .50-caliber machine guns, accounted for 8,302 of them, more than all other versions combined.
whyItMatters: Bombers flying deep into Europe needed fighters to protect them, and early escorts could not go the whole way. The Mustang's first engine, an Allison, lost power at altitude. Rolls-Royce and fighter pilots who had flown the airplane urged a switch to the Merlin, whose supercharger held sea-level power up to about 30,000 feet, and the Merlin-powered XP-51B was about 50 mph faster. Once P-51s could stay with the bombers for the entire mission, bomber losses dropped sharply.

The Mustang was the first single-engine fighter based in Britain to reach Berlin, and it escorted B-29s across the Pacific too. The Tuskegee Airmen, the first Black aviators allowed to fly for the US military, flew mostly P-51s with red-painted tails in the 332nd Fighter Group.

It also marks a handover. The Merlin came from the [Spitfire](/aircraft/supermarine-spitfire); the Mustang's successor as the fastest thing in the sky was the jet-powered [Me 262](/aircraft/messerschmitt-me-262), about 120 mph faster at the same altitude. The US Air Force did not retire its last P-51s until 1957.
facts: The P-51D's Packard-built Merlin V-1650 produced 1,695 horsepower and gave a top speed of 425 mph; the late-war P-51H reached 490 mph.
The wing spans 37 feet and the airplane is about 32 feet long; the Smithsonian's example weighs 7,635 pounds.
One weak point was the cooling system: the Smithsonian notes that a single bullet through a radiator or coolant pipe was usually enough to bring a Mustang down.
The Smithsonian's P-51D-30-NA, serial 44-74939, was delivered in July 1945, never saw combat and flew 211 hours before being set aside as a museum specimen.
In 1941 Charles "Chief" Anderson, who trained Black pilots at the Tuskegee Institute, took First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt flying when she visited.
